title: Bit Manipulation Mastery
description: Master binary representation, bitwise operators, shifts, masks, and efficient bit-manipulation techniques for algorithmic problem solving.

modules.title: Introduction to Bitwise Operator
modules.description: Master foundational principles and practical problem solving in Introduction to Bitwise Operator.

topics.title: Number systems (Binary and Decimal)
topics.description: Learn Number systems (Binary and Decimal) through focused explanations and practical bit-manipulation examples.

pages.title: Digits
pages.content:
A positional number system represents a value using a base. In decimal (base 10), the digit at position b contributes digit × 10^b.

For example:
`32510 = 3×10^4 + 2×10^3 + 5×10^2 + 1×10 + 0`.

Binary is base 2 and uses only `0` and `1`. Bit manipulation works directly with these binary positions.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

checkpoint.question: A fixed binary position represents a power of two; the rightmost bit is position 0.
options: A fixed binary position represents a power of two; the rightmost bit is position 0.
A bit operation changes unrelated data structure nodes automatically.
Binary search is the only way to inspect a bit.
checkpoint.explanation: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

pages.title: Bits
pages.content:
A binary number uses two digits: `0` and `1`. Starting from the right, bit positions are numbered `0, 1, 2, ...`.

For example, `10011101₂ = 128 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 157`.

The rightmost bit is the **LSB** (least significant bit); the leftmost set-position is the **MSB** (most significant bit).

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

pages.title: MCQ - Decimal Value
pages.content:
Convert binary `101₂` using powers of two:

`1×2^2 + 0×2^1 + 1×2^0 = 5`.

The important skill is reading each set bit as its corresponding power of two.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

pages.title: MCQ - Trailing Zeroes
pages.content:
Trailing zeroes are zero bits at the right end of a binary representation.

For example, `40` is `101000₂`, so it has three trailing zeroes. A trailing-zero count is useful because it identifies the position of the least significant set bit for positive integers.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

pages.title: MCQ - Convert to Binary
pages.content:
To convert a positive decimal integer to binary, repeatedly divide by 2 and record each remainder.

For example, `23` produces remainders `1,1,1,0,1` from right to left, giving `10111₂`.

Leading zeroes may be omitted when displaying an ordinary binary representation.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

pages.title: Bitwise Operators
pages.content:
Bitwise operators act on corresponding bits of integer operands.

- `A & B`: bit is 1 only when both bits are 1.
- `A | B`: bit is 1 when either bit is 1.
- `A ^ B`: bit is 1 when the bits differ.

These operations let algorithms manipulate flags, masks, and compact state efficiently.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Binary representation is positional: bit b contributes 2^b when it is set.

topics.title: Bitwise Operators - 1 (AND, OR, XOR)
topics.description: Learn Bitwise Operators - 1 (AND, OR, XOR) through focused explanations and practical bit-manipulation examples.

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise AND OR
pages.content:
Compare the bits independently.

For example:
`10111 & 101101` first aligns the values by position, while `|` keeps every bit set in either operand.

The key idea is that AND is restrictive, while OR is accumulative.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

checkpoint.question: AND keeps only bits set in both operands; OR keeps bits set in at least one operand; XOR keeps bits that differ.
options: AND keeps only bits set in both operands; OR keeps bits set in at least one operand; XOR keeps bits that differ.
A bit operation changes unrelated data structure nodes automatically.
Binary search is the only way to inspect a bit.
checkpoint.explanation: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise AND
pages.content:
For `C = A & B`, each bit of C is set only if the corresponding bits of **both** A and B are set.

Therefore, `A & B` cannot contain a set bit that is absent from either operand.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise OR
pages.content:
For `C = A | B`, each bit of C is set if the corresponding bit of **at least one** operand is set.

Therefore, the set bits of both inputs are combined into the result.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise XOR
pages.content:
XOR returns `1` exactly when the two corresponding bits differ.

Useful identities include:
`x ^ 0 = x`
`x ^ x = 0`
`x ^ y ^ y = x`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Bitwise XOR Again
pages.content:
XOR is both associative and commutative. This means:

`a ^ b ^ c` has the same value regardless of the order in which the operands are combined.

That property makes XOR useful for cancelling paired values.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: Dull Operation
pages.content:
A common bit trick is `n & (n - 1)`.

For any positive integer n, it clears the lowest set bit:
`12 = 1100₂`
`11 = 1011₂`
`12 & 11 = 1000₂ = 8`.

For `n = 0`, handle the edge case separately.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - OR Operation with 1 Less
pages.content:
The expression `n | (n - 1)` has a predictable effect on the low-order bits.

For an odd n, the least significant bit is already 1, so `n | (n - 1)` equals `n`.

Bit identities like this are useful for fast reasoning about binary patterns.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - XOR Operation With 1 Less
pages.content:
The expression `n ^ (n - 1)` highlights the low-order bits around the least significant set bit.

For an odd n, `n - 1` changes the least significant 1 to 0 and all lower zero bits do not exist; the resulting XOR therefore produces the low bit pattern `1` at minimum.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Bitwise operators act independently on corresponding bit positions.

topics.title: Bitwise Operators - 2 (NOT, LEFT and Right Shifts)
topics.description: Learn Bitwise Operators - 2 (NOT, LEFT and Right Shifts) through focused explanations and practical bit-manipulation examples.

pages.title: MCQ - Left Shift Operation
pages.content:
A left shift moves bits toward more significant positions. For a non-negative integer without overflow, `n << b` equals `n × 2^b`.

A right shift moves bits toward less significant positions. For a positive integer, `n >> b` is floor(n / 2^b).

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Use masks such as 1 << b to inspect and modify individual bit positions.

checkpoint.question: A left shift by b multiplies a non-negative value by 2^b when no relevant bits are discarded; a right shift moves bits toward lower positions.
options: A left shift by b multiplies a non-negative value by 2^b when no relevant bits are discarded; a right shift moves bits toward lower positions.
A bit operation changes unrelated data structure nodes automatically.
Binary search is the only way to inspect a bit.
checkpoint.explanation: Use masks such as 1 << b to inspect and modify individual bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Left Shift on 1
pages.content:
`1 << B` creates a mask with exactly one set bit at position B.

Examples:
`1 << 0 = 1`
`1 << 3 = 8`
`1 << 5 = 32`.

This is the standard building block for testing, setting, and toggling a bit.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Use masks such as 1 << b to inspect and modify individual bit positions.

pages.title: MCQ - Right Shift Operation
pages.content:
For positive integers, `A >> B` shifts the binary representation right by B positions.

Each shift discards a low-order bit and moves every remaining bit one position lower. Repeated right shifts therefore divide a positive integer by powers of two using integer arithmetic.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: Use masks such as 1 << b to inspect and modify individual bit positions.

topics.title: Conceptual Problems
topics.description: Learn Conceptual Problems through focused explanations and practical bit-manipulation examples.

pages.title: MCQ - OR of Array
pages.content:
A cumulative OR combines the set bits present anywhere in an array.

Starting with `result = 0`, apply `result |= value` for every element. The final result contains a 1 in every bit position set by at least one input.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

checkpoint.question: Bit tricks are useful when a problem can be expressed as independent decisions on individual bits.
options: Bit tricks are useful when a problem can be expressed as independent decisions on individual bits.
A bit operation changes unrelated data structure nodes automatically.
Binary search is the only way to inspect a bit.
checkpoint.explanation: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: MCQ - XOR of Two Numbers
pages.content:
XOR compares two integers bit by bit. A result bit is 1 when exactly one input bit is 1.

For example, `9 ^ 12 = 01001₂ ^ 01100₂ = 00101₂ = 5`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: Weapon Value
pages.content:
Each participant owns a 10-bit weapon string. When two participants battle, equal weapon types cancel and different weapon types survive; this is exactly a bitwise XOR.

Because XOR is associative and commutative, the final weapon set is the XOR of all participant strings. The requested weapon value is the number of set bits in that final string.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: MCQ - Which Bitwise Operator
pages.content:
Choose the operator from the operation you need:
- common set bits → `&`
- combine set bits → `|`
- difference/cancellation → `^`
- invert every bit → `~`.

Choosing the operation from the required bit behavior is more reliable than memorizing examples.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: MCQ - XOR Properties
pages.content:
Three identities make XOR especially useful:

- `x ^ 0 = x`
- `x ^ x = 0`
- `x ^ y ^ x = y`

Repeated values can therefore cancel, which is the basis of several linear-time XOR algorithms.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: MCQ - Powers of Two
pages.content:
For a positive integer n, n is a power of two exactly when only one bit is set.

A compact test is:
`(n & (n - 1)) == 0`.

The `n > 0` check is necessary because zero also satisfies `n & (n - 1) == 0`.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

pages.title: MCQ - Minimum Operations
pages.content:
Bitwise operations can often reduce an apparently large state space to independent bit decisions.

For example, if one operation can handle every array element having the same power-of-two bit, the total number of required operations is determined by the number of distinct bit positions involved.

callout.title: Key Takeaway
callout.text: XOR is associative and commutative, so many pairwise XOR processes reduce to one cumulative XOR.

practiceProblems.description: Choose one non-negative integer X to append to an array so that the bitwise OR of the whole array contains every bit set in a target mask.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Read N, the array A, and a target mask M. Find the smallest non-negative X such that (A1 | A2 | ... | AN | X) equals M. If the existing OR already contains a bit outside M, print -1.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N and M. Second line: N integers.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print the smallest valid X, or -1 if no solution exists.

sampleTestCases.explanation: The current OR is 7, so appending 8 produces 15.

practiceProblems.title: Weapon Value
practiceProblems.description: N participants each own a 10-bit weapon string. Combining two participants uses XOR: weapons present in both are destroyed, while weapons present in exactly one remain. Find the maximum possible number of weapon types in the final winner.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Read N binary strings of length 10. Because XOR is associative and commutative, the final weapon string is the XOR of all participant strings. Print the number of 1s in that result.
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line: N. Next N lines: binary strings of length 10.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: Print the maximum possible number of remaining weapon types.

practiceProblems.title: Make Them Zero
practiceProblems.description: An operation chooses any subsequence and subtracts a positive power of two from every selected element. Determine the minimum number of operations required to turn the entire array into zero.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Read an array of non-negative integers. In one operation, choose any set of indices whose current values are large enough and subtract the same power of two from those indices. Output the minimum number of operations needed to make every value zero.
constraints: Sum of N over test cases <= 2*10^5
practiceProblems.inputFormat: First line T. For each test case: N, then N integers.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case print the minimum number of operations.

sampleTestCases.explanation: Each operation can process all elements sharing the chosen power-of-two bit.
